read-2026-09-13-the-git-risk-and-what-i-: The risk that ate two recipes — and the part of my own diagnosis that was wrong
13 Sep 2026. Nothing here has been changed. This is a description, not a fix.
First: I named the wrong culprit
In the plan I wrote yesterday I said this:
"your allow-list contains pre-approved git -C ~/testing stash push -u — and stash push -u sweeps up untracked files."
I read the rule properly today. It cannot do that.
It is an exact-match rule tied to one dead session. It auto-approves one literal command that will never be typed again. It did not cause the loss, and it is not a standing risk.

So the honest position is: two recipes were orphaned by a git operation during the repo consolidation, and I do not know which one. I recovered them. I cannot name the cause, and I am not going to invent one twice.
What the audit actually found — all 31 rules, read today
31 auto-approved. Zero blocked. Zero set to ask.
Most are harmless — reading a Notion page, checking a yt-dlp version, taking a browser screenshot. Three are not narrow, and they are worth your eye:
Bash(python -c ' *)
Run any Python at all, no prompt. The * is the whole language
claude desktoi
Bash(git apply *)
Apply any patch to any file
home folder
Read(//c/Users/soyan/**)
Read anything in your user folder
claude desktoi
python -c '* is the widest one by a distance. Everything a delete, an upload or an overwrite needs is inside Python. An AI that wanted to do any of those has a door that does not knock.
I am not saying anything abused it. I am saying the door has no lock and you never chose that — it was accumulated one "always allow" click at a time.
The three options, and what each costs you
I have implemented none of them. Each changes how your machine behaves when you are not watching, and that is your call, not mine.
If you only do one, do the deny list. It costs you nothing in daily friction, because it blocks only things you would never authorise anyway.
What is safe right now, measured
All ten recipes
on disk, tracked in git, committed
The same ten
in Google Drive → READ BEFORE WORK
Untracked recipe files
none — that was the exposed state, and it is closed
The specific thing that bit us cannot bite the same way again: a tracked, committed, pushed, Drive-copied file has four homes. The lost pair had one.
The lesson worth keeping

When you find recoverable work in a dangling commit, recover it immediately. Do not write a plan about it first. I wrote the plan. The garbage collector ran. I had to write both recipes again from the transcripts.

The test: open Outlook or Teams at work and look for a Copilot button. If it is there, this course is about your job. If not, skip the whole thing.
I am not going to guess which. You have a full-time job and I do not know what software it runs on.
🚨 If you DO use it at work — read this part first, before anything else
Sabrina: "can your company see all of your chats?" Sheree: "Yes, your company actually can."
Her actual examples of what not to type:
"don't type 'my boss is a jerk, what should I say to him'" "don't type 'how much is my coworker making'"
This is the single most useful thing in two hours, and it is 90 seconds long. It is safe for company files. It is not private for you.
The six agents — what each one is for
Her framing: you stop asking questions and start handing over tasks.
"We're used to going back and forth. It's like a partner... But nowadays we're moving into the world of agents. You're just giving it a task to do."
Facilitator
Sits in your meeting. Takes the notes, pulls the action items, schedules the follow-ups. "You don't need" a separate note-taker
Researcher
Digs through your files and the web
Analyst
"every employee has access to an expert agent able to perform complex multi-step data analysis" — she calls it "analyst level work... a step up"
Prompt coach
"the most underrated agent that there is" — you tell it what you are trying to do and it writes the prompt
Idea coach
Brainstorming
Writing / visual
Drafting and images
The prompt coach is the one worth knowing about even if you never use Copilot — the idea that you describe the goal and something else writes the prompt.
Four features worth stealing, whatever tool you use
1 · Temporary chat — ignore your own standing instructions, just this once
"Maybe you have your custom instructions that you wanted to break things down very simply, but for this one time you don't want that... temporary chat will literally ignore your custom instructions.
A lot of people don't even know that exists."
You have 62 standing rules that apply to every reply. There is no way to say "not this time" without arguing with them. That is a genuinely good idea and you do not have it.
2 · Scheduled prompts
"you could say over the weekend, take all the emails that I've received and put them in order to what's most important."
Save a prompt once, have it run Monday morning.
3 · The prompt gallery

"How many people have said 'I don't know how to write a prompt'... all you have to do is drop down here and you're going to see all these prompts. And these prompts are going to actually pull from your work."
Her example: "Help me prepare for a one-on-one" pulls every relevant Word file, meeting and Teams message. "Instead of spending 30 minutes... I can prepare for a meeting within like 5 seconds."
4 · A work/web toggle
One switch: answer from my company's files, or answer from the internet. Simple, and most tools make you say it in words every time.
Two things in here that are quietly interesting
Copilot is other people's models wearing a Microsoft badge

"The GPT models are right here. So you can get either GPT 5.2 think deeper or GPT 5.2 quick response. Co-Pilot is built on the back of that and most people don't even understand that. And for the agents...
those are actually built on the back end of Claude."
So "which AI is best" matters less than you would think — the same models are inside several products you might be choosing between.
Her model-setting advice, which is sensible anywhere
"I would advise them to just have it default to auto... if you think it's taking too long then go to quick response, or if you think the responses aren't good enough, then go to think deeper."
Do not pick the most powerful setting by default. Pick it when the answer disappoints you.

recipe-11-loop-engineering.html: RECIPE 11 — Loop engineering: /goal and routines
From: Loop Engineering, Claude Code /goal, and Agent Routines · 19 Jun 2026 · 1:46:04 · watch

Worked examples from: 6 INSANE Projects to Learn Claude Fable and /goal · 10 Jul 2026 · 1:47:17 livestream · and its 13-minute cut, Claude Fable 6 INSANE Projects To Get Ahead of 99% · 3 Aug 2026 · 13:29
A loop is three things: do a step, check it against a finish line you wrote down, then go again or stop. /goal runs that loop while you watch. A routine runs it on a timer in the cloud.
The hard part, she says, is the checker. Her own checker is the part that breaks your rules.
THE ONE THING — write the finish line before the task
Her shape for every /goal prompt, from her cheat sheet:
Her first demo sorted her Downloads folder into subfolders by type. The prompt ended:
"Keep going until no files are left. Do not delete anything. And stop after 30 turns." (27:30)
She names three things that made it a good goal: a clear end state, a check it can run, and a guardrail. The turn limit is her token brake.
In July she stretched it to five parts: task, why, outcome, constraints, verification. Verification matters most (9:00).
"actually the hardest part is defining the checker" (21:01)
Why this matters to you
In most chats today, you are the loop. I say something is done, and you decide whether it is. Her whole case for a separate checker is one you already hold:
"the first agent is just biased and will lie to you" (11:01)
A written finish line means your review starts from a number, not from my word.
The checker problem — her setup breaks your rule
She says it three times:
"such as a cheaper model like Haiku checking and reviewing the work independently" (16:32)
"default checker in cloud code is haiku. You can change it so it uses a different model" (23:02)
"I believe the default is Hi Q." (24:31)
This is NOT confirmed. She states it flatly in June and says "I believe" in July. Neither video shows a setting, a document or how to change it.
Treat the checker's model as unknown until you have read /goal's own help text.
Two fixes, both built from her own advice:
Make "checked by" something a plain command can count. Her own question is "Is it a count?" Then the checker only reads a number. It never has to judge quality.
Never treat "goal achieved" as a pass. Have a strong model or a script recount before you believe it. For routines, the form has a model picker (42:00), so give the checker routine a strong model.
How /goal works, in her words
She says /goal wraps the Stop hook: "it runs that a small prompt at the end of each cloud code" turn (26:31). /goal clear stops it. Typing /goal while it runs gives a status update (1:05:31).
You run your own hooks. Neither video tests /goal alongside other hooks, so try your first goal in a scratch folder.
A loose finish line, caught on camera
In July she trained a simulated spider to climb stairs. The goal passed. The staircase had about three steps.
"technically the verification step is correct" ... "make sure there's 20 stairs instead of like three" (46:31)
In June she gave the same warning about code: your "end condition was make sure all the tests pass but your tests were garbage" (58:30).
This is the grader pattern from Recipe 04, failing the way it fails. The gate is only as good as what it counts.
Routines — the same loop on a timer
A routine is a saved loop. It runs in the cloud "even when your laptop is closed" (39:02), in a fresh environment that pulls your GitHub project.
The form has these fields:
a name and instructions
a GitHub project, which is optional
a model
a trigger: a schedule, a GitHub webhook or a POST request (40:30)
connectors
environments, which hold API keys (50:01)
Her real maker and checker pair, for her support inbox:
Her safety advice is to start read-only: "let it summarize stuff for a few days before you let it write anything" (56:00).
For connector permissions she suggests "always allow for read only things" and approval for any write, edit or delete (45:31).
For a loop that stays on your own machine, she points Mac users to launchd (39:31). She does not demo it.
Each of these needs your yes first:
connecting Gmail, Slack or any account to a cloud routine
putting an API key into a cloud environment
any routine that sends, closes, edits or posts something
her marketing demo's last step, "Claude post everything" (54:00), which is public posting

Neither video gives a price per /goal run. It spends your plan allowance.

recipe-12-live-search-data-in-claude-cod: RECIPE 12 — Live search data in Claude Code
From: How to do Keyword Research in Claude Code (Goodbye Semrush) · 24 Mar 2026 · 17:39 · watch
From: How I Built an AI SEO Agent to Rank #1 in 10 Minutes (Claude Code) · 23 May 2026 · 20:40 · watch
Two creators plug the same paid data service, DataForSEO, into Claude Code so it can read real search numbers instead of guessing them. The idea is sound. The data is Google's, not Etsy's.
Read this first

Ryan sells his keyword skill and skips the setup, saying it is in another video. Sandy's video is sponsored by DataForSEO, and the site she audits and fixes is her own. So neither video shows the whole build.
The build below fills the gaps from DataForSEO's own setup page and Claude Code's own help text, both read on 16 Sep 2026. It needs neither the paid skill nor the missing video.
THE ONE THING — don't ask a model for numbers it doesn't have
Ask Claude "what do people search for?" and it gives a confident answer from memory. Ryan's point is that the model is not reading live data.
"they're not up-to-date 24/7"
(2:32) Connect a data service, and the same question comes back with real columns. His came back with monthly search volume, keyword difficulty and cost per click (7:31).
Why this matters to you
Your rules say research comes before building, with a demand figure read this month and dated. This is a way to get that figure inside Claude Code, dated, without opening another tool.

But be clear about what it does not touch. You already rank #2 on Etsy AU for "dementia caregiver binder", and you have zero sales. Your gap is what happens after someone sees a listing. Search data can't see that.
This recipe is for choosing and wording the NEXT product, not for fixing the current one.
THE BIG CAVEAT — this is Google, not Etsy
Everything both videos pull is Google search (and AI chatbot answers). Your Etsy ranking was measured by searching Etsy itself, logged out. That is still the only way to know where you rank on Etsy.
I searched DataForSEO's docs index page on 16 Sep 2026 for "etsy" and found nothing. It does list Google, Bing and Amazon.
How often a phrase is searched on Google, by country
How often it is searched on Etsy
Which wording people use: "caregiver binder" vs "care planner"
Where your listing ranks in Etsy search
Whether a phrase is growing or shrinking over 12 months
Whether an Etsy shopper clicks, favourites or buys
What pages Google shows for a phrase, which may include Etsy listings
Why your listings have zero sales
What ChatGPT or Gemini recommend when asked
Anything about Etsy ads or Etsy's own algorithm
Google volume is a fair proxy for "does this need exist, and what do people call it". It isn't a proxy for Etsy demand.
How each video builds it
Ryan: a keyword skill
Write a keyword research skill. He sells his, but says to write your own first (1:31).
Connect DataForSEO or Ahrefs (3:32).
Ask the skill for keywords on a root topic, then tell it which rows you dislike and which columns to add. That updates the skill as you go (8:30).
Hand a chosen keyword to a writing skill (9:00).
"Use my keyword research skill to find me 15 relevant and intentful keyword ideas based on the root topic of Claude code marketing."
The gap: at step 2 he says "I have a full other video showing you how to set this up, so I'm not going to do that in this video.
" (5:30) All you see is the idea: paste DataForSEO's documentation link into Claude Code and ask for help, then give it your API login.
Sandy: an "SEO agent" loop
Get an API login and password from DataForSEO. The password is emailed (6:00).
Paste a setup command with them into Claude Code, then check it with a list command (7:00). The command is on screen, not in the captions. They only say to paste "this right here".
Give Claude a research prompt (8:30). She reads out part of it: who AI engines recommend in her niche, search volumes and trends, a Google AI overview check, and competitor patterns.
The full prompt is a skill she gives by email or in her paid community.
Have Claude fix the site. She calls this the step most people skip (11:30).
Re-run the audit. She went from F to D (19:00).
Steps 4 and 5 need a website whose code you control. An Etsy listing isn't one, so for you they stop at step 3. She also says AI engines take "about 14 to 21 days" to notice changes (12:02).
So her F-to-D score comes from her own audit tool, not from AI engines naming her.
The build, rewritten — no paid skill, no missing video
Signing up, accepting DataForSEO's terms and adding credit are yours to do. So is typing the password. Keep it out of the chat.

The setup, from DataForSEO's own GitHub page (read 16 Sep 2026): they run a hosted server at https://mcp.dataforseo.com/v3/mcp, and it signs in with OAuth. That means a browser login instead of a pasted password.
Claude Code's own claude mcp add --help shows the matching command:

Then type /mcp in Claude Code, pick dataforseo and choose authenticate. Ryan does exactly that for Ahrefs (13:01). I haven't run this on your machines. Check it by reading /mcp back before trusting it.
The GitHub page also offers a local version that takes the login and password as settings. Sandy keeps hers in a .env file and changes the key often (10:02).
Money — every price the videos give
"you start with $1, which I know does not seem like a lot, which it is not."
"about maybe 5 to 10 cents per output"
$5 trial credit through her link, "instead of $1"
Sandy, May 2026, sponsored (5:30)
"It cost 3 cents, guys, for us to do this."
Sandy, May 2026, her whole research step (14:01)
Ahrefs API on its lowest plan, "$129 a month"; it was enterprise-only at about $1,500
SEO agencies at $5,000 to $20,000 a month
Sandy, May 2026 (13:00)

Ryan's 5 to 10 cents a run sits right on your 10c ask line. So every run needs a stated price first. Sandy says spending comes off a prepaid deposit (11:01), which should cap spending at the balance (not tested here).
Topping it up is money, so it goes to you.
Both creators run with bypass permissions (7:00, 17:31). With paid calls, that means no pause before spending. Ryan himself suggests plan mode the first time. See Recipe 09.
What to try — one step, tonight
Only if you are choosing the next product. It does nothing for the current zero-sales problem.
The prompt:
Using only the DataForSEO MCP, get Google search volume in Australia, with a 12-month trend, for these 10 phrases: [your phrases]. Before any paid call, state the endpoint and estimated cost.
After it, report the real cost from the API response. Label the result "Google, not Etsy", with today's date.
Then search the best two phrases on Etsy yourself, logged out, the way you measured your rankings. The Google number says the need exists. Only the Etsy search says who you'd be up against.
ALSO MENTIONED
Ryan uses Ahrefs for backlink checks, his own and competitors' (16:02). You need a paid Ahrefs account for any of it.
After changing data services, he had to update the skill to use the new one (13:30).
Sandy's reason for live data: chatbot answers are personalised to your past chats (4:31).
Sandy says "Almost 77% of the people in the US" use AI instead of Google to search (2:02). She gives no source.
Asking ChatGPT or Gemini through DataForSEO is a third-party route. It isn't your Vertex route for Gemini, so decide whether that's allowed before you use it.

Connect Canva inside claude.ai, clone a template you already like, and make Claude count the words in every text box before it writes anything. The design survives because the copy is cut to fit it.
Read this first
All three videos are by Sabrina Ramonov, and the posting half sells her own app, Blotato. You can skip that half. The making half is free on claude.ai with a free Canva account.
The second title says 200 posts. On screen she makes one Instagram post from scratch and one seven-slide carousel. That is all.
THE ONE THING — count the words before you replace them
She does not ask Claude to "make a flyer". She clones a Canva template, pastes its link, and reads out this prompt:
"Analyze the following Canva template, especially the number of words per section."
"Then ask me questions to replace the text with my information, roughly following the number of words per section."
Her reason, at 8:00:
"if you were to replace this with like five sentence paragraph, it just wouldn't look good."
A human designed the template, so the layout already works. Claude only has to respect it.
Why this matters to you
Your shop is found. You rank #2 on Etsy AU for "dementia caregiver binder", with 46 live listings and zero sales as of 12 Sep 2026. So the unproven part is what happens after someone sees a listing.
Listing images are part of that. This recipe does not prove your images are the problem; nothing here measures that.
It gives you a cheap way to make one alternative image from a template you chose, so you have something to test.
It also fits your rule against code-drawn art. The design comes from a Canva template a person made. Claude only writes the words into it.
How it goes, step by step
1. Connect Canva (once)
In claude.ai: your name, bottom left, then Settings, then Connectors. Browse connectors, search Canva, press +, and allow (1:00). She says you do not need Cowork, Desktop or Claude Code for this.
Then press Configure. Each Canva action is marked always allow or needs approval, and you can switch any of them (2:30).
Connecting grants Canva access to your account. That is your click, not mine.
2. Ask what the connector can do
Her "product tour" prompt, from the second video at 2:01:
"List every Canva connector feature available. Output a bullet point list with a sample prompt for each feature and Canva plan required."
It returns a table of features, sample prompts, and free versus paid.
3. Clone a template, then fill it
In Canva: Home, Templates, search (flyer, carousel, infographic), pick one, press "Customize this template". That makes your own editable copy (7:30). Paste its link into the prompt above.
She shows three ways to feed it the facts:
Claude interviews you
answered its questions for a hiring flyer
A topic only
"nature heals founders" for a carousel
Your website
"replace the text with information from my website"
For the carousel she approves each slide's copy before Claude builds it.
4. Open it in Canva and look
Everything saves to your Canva account and stays in sync. Hand edits in Canva are fine (17:01).
The fit is rough, not exact. In the second video one slide's text was "a little much" and overlapped, so she fixed it by hand (7:30). Claude had already flagged it:
"Claude actually said the subtitle positioning slightly overlaps with the text."
Read Claude's notes before you open the design. She did not, and it had caught the fault.
Swapping in your own photos
She uploads her photos into the chat and asks Claude to swap the backgrounds (12:30). Two limits:
A landscape photo in a portrait slot failed: "It was not able to handle that horizontal photo that I was just testing out". Match the photo's shape to the slot.
Her method runs through Blotato: "If you haven't set up Blotato yet, this obviously won't work." Without it, she warns, Claude tries workarounds and may hit problems.
So the photo swap is the one part the video only shows working with the paid app. It shows no free way. Uploading photos into Canva yourself might work, but that is my guess and it is untested.
If it is a product photo, the image must not change what the buyer gets. Swapping a background is one thing. Changing a page, a page count or a feature is misrepresentation.
The two error fixes, word for word
She says the two errors are related, and both fixes name Blotato.
Canva export domain "not in my sandbox's network allow list" (12:30)
"export from Canva and then pass the Canva export domain URLs directly to Blotato to post" (20:00)
Claude stuck uploading your photos, or trying to start an HTTP server (13:30)
"use Blotato to upload my photos or videos so Canva can use them" (20:31)
She says the reason the second works is that Blotato "has a media library endpoint". Once it works, she tells Claude to remember the fix.
Without Blotato, neither fix applies. For your use you do not need the first. Export the PNG or PDF from Canva by hand. Claude's own reply on screen offers PNG or PDF export (5:01).
Money, and what needs your yes
claude.ai with the Canva connector
no price given
Canva
"Many features will still work with a free Canva account"
Canva brand kit
paid: "Notice it has this crown icon, which means it requires a paid plan." No figure given
Blotato posting
"It does require a paid plan of $29 per month"
Blotato, second video
"the lowest plan of $29 per month", 20 social accounts, "as of today, May 2026"
Blotato is her own app. Its "full refund, no questions asked" offer and its benefits have only her word behind them.
Posting is public. In the demo, Claude posted to Facebook and Instagram "right now". When Instagram rejected the size, Claude and Canva worked around it on their own with a square crop (21:31).
Her own verdict: "I probably shouldn't have posted this really long infographic to Instagram." Any post goes to you first.
Not covered in any of the three videos: whether Canva's licence lets you use community templates in paid Etsy listing images. Check Canva's terms before a template goes on a listing.
What to try — one image, tonight
Cost: nothing beyond the claude.ai plan you already use. No API call, no Blotato.
Every number on the image must match the file the buyer downloads. Take the page count from the built PDF, not from memory.
Whether it looks premium is a judgement. Look at it yourself, and do not let a cheap model sign it off.
ALSO MENTIONED
Designs from scratch: Canva offers four options, you pick one and ask for changes in chat (4:31)
A paid Canva brand kit (logo, colours, fonts) that Claude can use. She keeps several kits for several clients (23:31)
Blotato's calendar queue for scheduling batches of posts (19:30)
She adds Blotato as a custom connector at mcp.blotato.com/mcp (18:30)
Of the connector's features: "We really only touched the surface" (14:00)
The captions mishear Blotato many ways ("Vota", "Bloop to", "blue potato"). Quotes here keep only lines where it came through correctly

RECIPE 10 is the wider social automation family.
recipe-14-the-tiktok-30-day-sprint.html: RECIPE 14 — The TikTok sprint, and the search-gap tool inside it
From: Blow Up on TikTok in 30 Days · 27 Jan 2026 · 23:02 · watch
From: I Blew Up My TikTok Following As Fast As I Could! · 8 Feb 2025 · 24:24 · watch
Two Sabrina videos teach one plan: pick one topic, post 100 short videos fast, copy proven hooks, and aim at the searches TikTok says nobody is filling. The full sprint does not fit your week.
The search-gap tool fits tonight, and you do not have to post anything to use it.
These sit under your strongest comment on her list (11 Sep): "one of the things that I want to have another look at".
The newer video is from January 2026 and the older one from February 2025. TikTok moves its menus often. Every click path below is hers, as shown then, and may have moved.
THE ONE THING — TikTok tells you what people search for and cannot find
Her name for it is Creator Search Insights. It shows what people type into TikTok search, with numbers, and a "content gap" tab for searches that have too few videos.
"Tik Tok is literally asking you to make content on those topics so it can serve it to the people searching for it" (14:30)
Her path, February 2025 (15:00):
Then the rule that she says moved her from about 200 views to thousands: use the exact phrase everywhere. Title, description, hashtags, and said out loud (07:31).
Her check that it worked: open your own video and look at the search bar at the top.
"you don't want it to say find related Concept in the top search bar here" (07:00)
She ran it on seven videos in two days. The captions read "23 9,000 views in the past 48 hours" (18:33). That is probably 239,000, but auto-captions garble numbers, so treat it as unverified.
It was also on an AI account that already had a large following.
Why this matters to you
Your listings can already be found. You rank #2 on Etsy AU for "dementia caregiver binder". What is unproven is what happens after someone sees a listing.
So a TikTok sprint pushes on exposure, which is not your measured gap. Be honest about that before spending hours.

But the search tool helps with the other side. It shows the exact words caregivers type, with numbers, for free. That is buyer language for titles and first lines, gathered before you build or rewrite anything.
The full sprint — what she actually asks for
One topic only
"If you want to experiment with other topics, do it on another account"
Study hooks
Scroll viral videos in your niche and watch only the first 5–10 seconds
Copy the hook
Same words, colour, position and size, with your own content
Keep it short
Under 30 seconds, so flops do not burn you out
Hashtags
3–5 relevant ones, reused, ideally over 500,000 uses
Reply fast
15–30 minutes answering every comment after posting
Remake winners
Same format, new topic
Volume
100 videos in 30 days, "roughly 3 to four videos every single day"
Her reason for the volume: "volume negates luck" (02:02). The 2025 video adds "do not use automation" for the first 100 (03:32).
The honest time sum
Her own figure: "usually doesn't take me more than 15, max 20 minutes per video" (22:00). That is her speed, as a creator with 680,000 followers.
That does not fit a full-time job. She says so herself:
"if Tik Tok is not going to be your primary Channel then you don't need to do this" (08:00)
Where the two videos disagree, or overclaim
Shadowban line. The 2026 video says fewer than 100 views on 10 videos in a row (20:00). The 2025 video says "10 videos in a row each video fewer than 50 views" (13:00).
Both agree that about 200 views means a healthy account.
"you will be successful guaranteed" (09:31). Nobody can promise that.
"up to 30% of traffic comes from people searching on Tik Tok" (13:30). That is her own viral videos only.
Her fix for one stuck video is to set it private, restart the app, then set it public again (14:01). She shows no evidence it works.
She mentions rage bait and "visually jarring" props to get comments (18:02). That would be wrong for caregivers of people with dementia.
Money and permissions
Neither video gives a dollar price. The 2026 video's stance is:
"You don't need to pay for anything for this challenge." (21:31)
Her hook GPT ("Viral hooks for short videos") runs on a free ChatGPT account (07:00).
Her list of 1,000 hooks comes through her newsletter, so it costs you an email address (02:32).
The script workflow in the 2025 video runs inside Blotato, her own product. It calls the Perplexity API (20:30). No price is stated here, so under your rule nothing gets run until someone prices it.
Your call, not mine:
Posting anything on TikTok is public.
Face on camera is optional. She says talking head or faceless "doesn't matter" (03:32).
Anything that costs money.

If AI makes any image, voice or realistic footage in a video, use TikTok's AI-generated content label. Check TikTok's current rule before the first post, because it may have changed since these videos.
Show the real PDF pages, never code-drawn stand-ins.
What to try — one step, tonight
No posting, no money, about 20 minutes on your phone.
That gives you dated buyer language and costs nothing. Whether you ever post, it feeds straight into the part you have not proven: what someone reads after they find you.
If you later want to test posting — the smallest honest version
These numbers are my proposal, not hers. Posting is your decision.
Size
12 videos in 14 days, one topic (caregiver binders)
Each video
Under 30 seconds, title = one exact content-gap phrase
Time
Budget 20 minutes to make, 15 to reply ≈ 7 hours total
Real success
Any Etsy visits or favourites you can trace to TikTok
Signal only
2 or more of 12 pass 1,000 views (her "1, 5,000" unlock level)
Stop rule
After 12: most under 200 views and no Etsy visits → stop
Continue rule
A video clearly beats the rest → remake that format for 12 more
Views are not sales. Only the Etsy line counts as a result.
ALSO MENTIONED
Make a second account just to curate a For You feed of your niche, then scroll it for 30 minutes and note what stops you (01:31)
Templates she says work: listicles, "stop doing this", tutorials, breaking news (05:00)
Post at least three a day, one to two hours apart (08:30)
iPhone front camera, edit in the TikTok app, no makeup (09:02)
Her two regrets: not starting sooner, and not cross-posting to Instagram sooner (10:30)
One link in bio to a free lead magnet and email list, not a link tree (12:30)
TikTok's teleprompter effect for reading a script while filming (23:30)
Both transcripts are auto-captions. They reach her sign-off, but neither ends on a full stop.
See also
RECIPE 04 — hook frameworks and a word gate; its "three hooks, then pick" habit fits the posting test. RECIPE 05 — the audience playbook.
RECIPE 01 and RECIPE 10 — the automated Blotato side, which this plan says to avoid for the first 100 videos.
